## Positioning

Mission: Accelerate Entrepreneurs. Build. Advise. Invest.

Freedom with AI works with founders who have built the technology and now need to build the company. Space is the focus for both advising and investing. Advisory is also open to physical AI and deep-tech founders, and to a small number of FinTech, B2B software and life sciences engagements.

The firm brings operating, product and commercial experience, not aerospace engineering. Founders know the physics; the firm helps with who buys it, and how.

## Thesis

AI is leaving the screen, and space is its hardest test.

The money has moved in three steps, following Cammie Clay's State of AI: Investing talk:

- Bits (2010s to 2024): software eats the world through SaaS, apps and per-seat pricing. Investors rewarded growth and seats.
- Bits buy atoms (2025 to 2026): AI money pours into chips, data centers and power. Investors reward revenue and retention, not demos.
- Bits drive atoms (2027 and beyond): AI goes into the real world through robotaxis already on the road, then robots, devices and AI-designed drugs. Investors will reward a physical moat: hardware, real-world data and regulation.

The firm's focus is the next step: space. Software alone gets copied in months. Software plus the real world is hard to copy, and space is the hardest real world there is.

### The stack in space

The five-layer stack builds on Jensen Huang's framing of AI as infrastructure. The space mapping is the firm's own.

- Applications and embodied AI. On Earth: robots, vehicles, scientific tools and other systems that sense, decide and act. In space: imagery, connectivity, logistics and servicing in orbit.
- Models. On Earth: frontier, open-source and domain-specific models. In space: onboard autonomy, because spacecraft cannot wait for a round trip to Earth to make every decision.
- Infrastructure. On Earth: data centers, networking, cooling, orchestration and security. In space: downlinks, ground networks and compute in orbit.
- Chips and compute. On Earth: processors, memory, interconnects and supply. In space: compute that survives radiation, heat and a tight power budget.
- Energy. On Earth: the constraint under everything. In orbit: literally finite, with every subsystem competing for it.

### Why space

- The moat is physical. Hardware in orbit, real-world data and hard-won licenses are hard to copy.
- Every AI constraint is sharper. Power, compute, bandwidth and latency are tighter in space.
- The business is the bottleneck. Many space companies have the engineering; fewer have a clear first customer, a sales motion that survives procurement, and a story investors outside the sector can follow.

### The company-building layer

The firm does not design spacecraft, chips or power systems. Its work begins where a technical capability has to become a product, find a buyer and support a durable company. The sequence is capability, then product, then market, then an enduring business. Questions it works through:

- Which customer needs this capability badly enough to pay, and when
- Commercial, civil government or defense: which comes first
- Which technical capability creates a meaningful product advantage
- Which business model works with the costs, timelines and capital required
- Which partners, primes or supply constraints determine scale
- What investors and acquirers will examine, and whether the story is ready
- What should remain outside the company's scope

### How the firm participates

- Advise, led by Sonia Sarao: hands-on advisory for ISAM, space and deep-tech founders turning a working technology into a business.
- Invest, led by Cammie Clay: the firm's own capital in early-stage space companies, and physical AI where it meets space.
- Build: AI-native products run end to end by AI agents: faibuddy, plus gosolokit and advising.space (coming soon).

## Advisory

### Where the firm helps

Finding the market: commercial, civil government or defense customers first; mapping the capability to concrete customer problems; market and competitive research; business model and pricing on long timelines; positioning and the company narrative.

Building the product and the company: product strategy built around a core technology; the software, data and AI layer around the hardware; roadmap, cost and runway decisions; team and operating structure, including distributed teams; new products and business lines.

Selling into complex buyers: buying committees, champions and decision-makers; go-to-market motion and sales strategy; partnerships, primes and channels; customer segmentation and verticalization; pricing and packaging.

Raising and diligence: a fundraising narrative for investors new to the sector; Series A and B preparation; what investors and acquirers examine in diligence; regulatory and risk questions that shape the plan; transaction readiness.

### When founders bring the firm in

- The technology works, but the first commercial customer has not signed
- Government or commercial first, and the answer changes the whole roadmap
- Engineers understand the capability; buyers do not yet
- Investors outside the sector do not understand the market
- Sales run through buying committees, primes and procurement
- A raise, partnership or acquisition is approaching and the story is not ready

### Engagement model

Regular working sessions on the decisions in motion, direct access between sessions, and continuity from decision through execution. Engagements begin with a three- or six-month term; scope and fee reflect the priorities and level of involvement. Start at https://freedomwith.ai/advisory#start.

### Selected advisory work

- Early-stage space: the company is connecting its technical capabilities to customer needs and commercial opportunities. The firm advises the founders and is an investor in the company.
- Early-stage FinTech: the company was refining its problem, target market and business model while regulatory requirements shaped what the product could become.
- Growth-stage B2B software: the company needed its enterprise segments, product strategy and AI direction to reinforce the same business model.
- Early-stage life sciences: the company needed to align its target market and business model with the compliance requirements affecting the product and operating model.

These examples are anonymized and describe work actually performed.

## Investing

The firm writes early, small checks with its own money in space companies, and in physical AI where it meets space. Where a company needs deep aerospace or hardware diligence, it invests alongside specialist investors.

What it looks for:

- Technology that works, or is close, with a clear path to a paying customer
- Founders who know the physics and want help with the business
- Markets where software, data and AI compound a hardware advantage
- A round where the firm can be useful beyond the capital

Advisory and investing are separate decisions. Working with the firm does not require or promise an investment. Investing enquiries and introductions: https://freedomwith.ai/contact?topic=investing

## Partners

### Sonia Sarao, Co-founder, Advisory

Sonia has spent more than 20 years in enterprise software and financial-market infrastructure, including a decade at NYSE. She was the first product hire at Fluxx and rose to VP of Product and Engineering as recurring revenue grew roughly tenfold, then led product at Groove through its acquisition by Clari. She helped win multimillion-dollar enterprise deals, developed new product lines and vertical strategies, and supported Series A and B fundraising and three M&A diligence processes. She has built and led technical teams across the US, India, Kenya, Canada and Europe, and holds degrees in computer science and software engineering. She brings software, product and commercial experience to space companies, not aerospace engineering.

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/sonia-sarao/

### Cammie Clay, Co-founder, Investing

Cammie leads investing at Freedom with AI. She is a seasoned trader and public markets investor. She worked on both sides of financial regulation: enforcement and investigations at the New York Stock Exchange and FINRA, then compliance leadership at RS Investments and First Republic Bank, where she was VP of Compliance in private wealth management. She holds a Series 7. Her regulatory background is in financial markets; in space she brings a diligence, risk and governance lens rather than sector-specific licensing expertise.

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/cammieclay/
